An inline table-valued function declares its return type with {{c1::RETURNS TABLE}}.
column2:
The inline header does not list result columns. SQL Server derives the names and types from the SELECT that defines the result.
CREATE FUNCTION dbo.GetCustomerOrders (@CustomerID int)
RETURNS TABLE
AS
RETURN (
    SELECT OrderID, Status, TotalAmount
    FROM dbo.Orders
    WHERE CustomerID = @CustomerID
);
Review source

column1: In an inline table-valued function, {{c1::RETURN}} introduces the single SELECT query.
column2:
The RETURN introduces the query that supplies the result. An inline TVF does not need INSERT statements or a named return variable.
CREATE FUNCTION dbo.GetCustomerOrders (@CustomerID int)
RETURNS TABLE
AS
RETURN (
    SELECT OrderID, Status, TotalAmount
    FROM dbo.Orders
    WHERE CustomerID = @CustomerID
);
Review source

column1: SQL Server infers an inline table-valued function's output columns from its {{c1::SELECT list}}.
column2:
Alias a calculated expression so the returned table has a usable column name. Its expression also determines the result type.
CREATE FUNCTION dbo.GetCustomerOrders (@CustomerID int)
RETURNS TABLE
AS
RETURN (
    SELECT OrderID, Status, TotalAmount
    FROM dbo.Orders
    WHERE CustomerID = @CustomerID
);
Review source

column1: Declare a result table named @Result with one INT column, OrderID, using {{c1::RETURNS @Result TABLE (OrderID INT)}}.
column2:
The header defines a named table variable with one integer column. Populate it in the body, then return it. Fabric Warehouse does not support this form.
CREATE FUNCTION dbo.GetOrderNumbers (@CustomerID int)
RETURNS @Result TABLE (OrderID int)
AS
BEGIN
    INSERT INTO @Result (OrderID)
    SELECT OrderID FROM dbo.Orders
    WHERE CustomerID = @CustomerID;
    RETURN;
END;
Review source | Fabric Warehouse

column1: A multi-statement table-valued function can add rows to its declared return table using {{c1::INSERT}}.
column2:
INSERT adds rows to the local result table. It does not write to a permanent table or change application data.
CREATE FUNCTION dbo.GetOrderNumbers (@CustomerID int)
RETURNS @Result TABLE (OrderID int)
AS
BEGIN
    INSERT INTO @Result (OrderID)
    SELECT OrderID FROM dbo.Orders
    WHERE CustomerID = @CustomerID;
    RETURN;
END;
Review source

column1: A T-SQL multi-statement table-valued function places its processing statements inside a {{c1::BEGIN...END}} block.
column2:
BEGIN and END enclose the statements that build the result. The block is not a transaction declaration.
CREATE FUNCTION dbo.GetOrderNumbers (@CustomerID int)
RETURNS @Result TABLE (OrderID int)
AS
BEGIN
    INSERT INTO @Result (OrderID)
    SELECT OrderID FROM dbo.Orders
    WHERE CustomerID = @CustomerID;
    RETURN;
END;
Review source

column1: After filling its declared result table, a multi-statement table-valued function ends with {{c1::RETURN;}}.
column2:
Bare RETURN finishes the function and returns the rows already in the declared variable. Do not put a scalar expression after it.
CREATE FUNCTION dbo.GetOrderNumbers (@CustomerID int)
RETURNS @Result TABLE (OrderID int)
AS
BEGIN
    INSERT INTO @Result (OrderID)
    SELECT OrderID FROM dbo.Orders
    WHERE CustomerID = @CustomerID;
    RETURN;
END;
Review source

column1: Use dbo.GetCustomerOrders to fetch customer 1001's orders: SELECT OrderID FROM {{c1::dbo.GetCustomerOrders(1001)}};
column2:
The call passes 1001 as the input and supplies rows for FROM. The outer SELECT then chooses which returned fields to show.
SELECT OrderID
FROM dbo.GetCustomerOrders(1001)
WHERE Status = 'Completed';
Review source

column1: Filter a function's returned orders with SELECT OrderID FROM dbo.GetCustomerOrders(1001) {{c1::WHERE}} Status = 'Completed';
column2:
This outer filter keeps completed rows from the customer's result. The function remains reusable for callers that need other statuses.
SELECT OrderID
FROM dbo.GetCustomerOrders(1001)
WHERE Status = 'Completed';
Review source

column1: Calculate total spending with SELECT {{c1::SUM(TotalAmount)}} FROM dbo.GetCustomerOrders(1001);
column2:
SUM reads TotalAmount from the returned table, just as it can read that column from a regular table. The function itself need not perform the aggregation.
SELECT SUM(TotalAmount) AS Total
FROM dbo.GetCustomerOrders(1001);
Review source

column1: Exclude customers without orders using FROM Customers AS c {{c1::CROSS APPLY}} dbo.GetCustomerOrders(c.CustomerID) AS o;
column2:
The function receives the current customer's key. If it returns no rows for that key, CROSS APPLY contributes nothing for that customer.
SELECT c.CustomerID, o.OrderID
FROM dbo.Customers AS c
CROSS APPLY dbo.GetCustomerOrders(c.CustomerID) AS o;
Review source

column1: Keep customers without orders using FROM Customers AS c {{c1::OUTER APPLY}} dbo.GetCustomerOrders(c.CustomerID) AS o;
column2:
OUTER APPLY preserves the customer when the function returns no orders. The order fields are NULL unless a later filter removes the row.
SELECT c.CustomerID, o.OrderID
FROM dbo.Customers AS c
OUTER APPLY dbo.GetCustomerOrders(c.CustomerID) AS o;
Review source

column1: Return only matching line items: SELECT d.OrderID FROM Sales.OrderDetails AS d {{c1::INNER JOIN}} dbo.GetCustomerOrders(1001) AS o ON o.OrderID = d.OrderID;
column2:
The call uses a constant, so it does not need the other input's columns to run. The ON clause joins its returned OrderID values to line items.
SELECT d.OrderID
FROM dbo.OrderDetails AS d
INNER JOIN dbo.GetCustomerOrders(1001) AS o
    ON o.OrderID = d.OrderID;
Review source

column1: If a CROSS APPLY passes the same inputs for every customer and has no linking filter, it produces a {{c1::Cartesian product}}.
column2:
If the fixed function returns three rows, each customer pairs with those same three rows. There is no customer-specific input or join filter.
Review source

column1: Place TRY...CATCH for function-call errors in {{c1::the calling batch or procedure}}, not inside a table-valued function.
column2:
Wrap the calling statement in TRY when you need to handle a catchable error. The function body cannot contain a CATCH block.
Review source

column1: Interleaved execution improves eligible multi-statement table-valued function plans using the function's {{c1::actual row count}}.
column2:
The engine can learn the actual count on the first eligible execution and use it to optimize the rest of the plan. A cached plan can reuse that count.
Review source

column1: In SQL Server 2017 and later, interleaved execution for eligible multi-statement table-valued function queries requires compatibility level {{c1::140 or higher}}.
column2:
Compatibility level enables access to the feature on supported versions. The setting and the calling statement still determine whether it is used.
